scenes.heading: Data Catalog
scenes.subheading: The searchable inventory of your data
scenes.narration: A data catalog is a centralized, searchable inventory of an organization's datasets, their schemas, owners, and meaning, so people can find and trust the data they need.

scenes.heading: What a catalog captures
bullets: Lineage links to upstream and downstream
scenes.narration: A catalog stores technical metadata such as schemas, data types, and partition layouts so engineers know the shape of a dataset. It captures business metadata like plain-language definitions, owners, and classification tags so analysts understand what a field means. It tracks operational metadata such as freshness, row counts, and quality scores. And it links to lineage so users can see where a dataset comes from and what depends on it.

scenes.heading: Discovering data with a catalog
steps: Users search by term or tag
scenes.narration: Automated crawlers connect to warehouses and lakes to harvest technical metadata continuously. Data owners then enrich entries with descriptions, glossary terms, and classifications. When a user needs data, they search the catalog by keyword, tag, or business term. They preview the schema, sample rows, and quality signals to judge fitness, then request access and start using the dataset with confidence.

scenes.heading: With a catalog vs without
scenes.narration: With a well-maintained catalog, people discover and reuse existing datasets quickly, ownership and meaning are explicit, and duplicated effort drops sharply. Without one, knowledge lives in people's heads and in scattered chat messages, teams unknowingly rebuild the same datasets in conflicting ways, and stale, undocumented tables pile up. A catalog only pays off if ingestion is automated and owners are held accountable for keeping context current.

scenes.heading: Governance built on the catalog
scenes.narration: A catalog is also the backbone of governance. Classifying columns as sensitive or personal in the catalog drives downstream masking and access rules. Access policies can be attached directly to catalog assets so permissions travel with the data's description. A shared business glossary aligns everyone on what terms like active user actually mean. And certification badges let data stewards mark which datasets are trusted and official, steering consumers away from ad-hoc or deprecated copies.

scenes.text: A catalog is where governance and self-service meet; automate the harvesting but insist on human-curated meaning.
scenes.narration: A catalog is where governance and self-service analytics meet, so automate the metadata harvesting for coverage but insist on human-curated business meaning and ownership so the catalog stays trustworthy.
